decisions.mark: states that staleness is THREE distinguishable axes rather than one flag, and names them
decisions.detail: QUOTE: "`data` | sources changed", "`schema` | index built by a newer pipeline than this process", "`code` | process predates the source tree", and "`notices()` ... turns those into a list of `{axis, message}`, ordered data, schema, code." | WHY: The answer explicitly names three independent axes (data, schema, code), reported separately with their own remedies, rather than one stale flag. || QUOTE: "The three inputs are: **Data:** ... **Schema:** ... **Code:** ..." and "`notices()` ... turns those into a list of `{axis, message}`, ordered data, schema, code." | WHY: The answer explicitly says staleness has three independent axes (data, schema, code), each reported separately with its own remedy. || QUOTE: "The three inputs are:" followed by "**Data:** ...", "**Schema:** ...", "**Code:** ..." and "reports each one as its own "axis" with a remedy" | WHY: The answer says staleness is three independent axes (data, schema, code), each reported separately with its own remedy.

decisions.mark: explains that each axis is cleared by a DIFFERENT action — a rebuild for data, a client restart for code — which is why one flag would not have been enough
decisions.detail: QUOTE: `code` | process predates the source tree | restart the MCP client; rebuilding will not help | no, a restart (and data row: "`index(action='refresh')`... yes, a rebuild") | WHY: The answer lists different remedies per axis (rebuild vs. restart) but never states that this is why a single flag would not have been enough. || QUOTE: `code` | process predates the source tree | restart the MCP client; rebuilding will not help | no, a restart; also "`data` | sources changed | `index(action='refresh')` ... | yes, a rebuild" | WHY: The answer states that data is cleared by a rebuild and code by a restart, but never says this is why one flag would not have been enough.

decisions.mark: identifies that the schema axis can be UNRESOLVABLE — when the index is newer than the server, no rebuild clears it, because rebuilding re-stamps the same newer version
decisions.detail: QUOTE: The schema notice's direction matters. If the index is newer than the server, a rebuild re-stamps the same newer version and never clears the flag. | WHY: The answer explicitly states that when the index is newer than the server, rebuilding re-stamps the same newer version and never clears the schema flag. || QUOTE: "If the index is newer than the server, a rebuild re-stamps the same newer version and never clears the flag." | WHY: The answer explicitly states that when the index is newer than the server, rebuilding re-stamps the same newer version and cannot clear the schema staleness. || QUOTE: If the index is newer than the server, a rebuild re-stamps the same newer version and never clears the flag. | WHY: The answer explicitly states that when the index is newer than the server, rebuilding re-stamps the same newer version and doesn't clear the schema flag.

decisions.mark: states the read/write asymmetry on the code axis: READS stay current because query tools open the database per call, while a BUILD through a stale process writes old pipeline logic
decisions.detail: QUOTE: `code` | process predates the source tree | restart the MCP client; rebuilding will not help ... The code notice says the query data is current even though the logic is old. ... `stale_code_refusal` blocks writes from a stale process and ignores `force`. | WHY: The answer says reads/query data stay current despite old logic, and that writes from a stale-code process are refused (an auto-refresh never writes an index with old logic), which covers the read/write asymmetry. || QUOTE: "`code` | process predates the source tree | restart the MCP client; rebuilding will not help" and "The code notice says the query data is current even though the logic is old." and "`stale_code_refusal` blocks writes from a stale process and ignores `force`." and "`_data_stale` returns false if the process predates its source, so an auto-refresh never writes an index with old logic." | WHY: The answer states that on the code axis the query data stays current while the logic is old, and that builds from a stale process are refused because they would write an index with old logic. That is the read/write asymmetry. || QUOTE: The code notice says the query data is current even though the logic is old. ... `stale_code_refusal` blocks writes from a stale process and ignores `force`. ... `_data_stale` returns false if the process predates its source, so an auto-refresh never writes an index with old logic. | WHY: The answer states that query data stays current while the process's logic is old, and that builds/writes from a stale-code process are refused because they would write an index with old logic.

decisions.mark: identifies that the write path REFUSES rather than warning, and that the refusal is placed ahead of the build decision so a force flag cannot override it
decisions.detail: QUOTE: `stale_code_refusal` blocks writes from a stale process and ignores `force`. The remedy is a client restart, then `index(action='refresh', force=True)`. | WHY: The answer states that the write path refuses (rather than warns) when the process code is stale and that `force` is ignored. That matches the item's refusal-that-force-cannot-override substance, though it does not spell out the placement ahead of the build decision. || QUOTE: `stale_code_refusal` blocks writes from a stale process and ignores `force`. The remedy is a client restart, then `index(action='refresh', force=True)`. | WHY: The answer states that the write path refuses (stale_code_refusal) and that it ignores `force`, which matches the item's substance of a refusal that a force flag cannot override. It does not say the refusal sits ahead of the build decision, but the force-immunity is stated. || QUOTE: `stale_code_refusal` blocks writes from a stale process and ignores `force`. The remedy is a client restart, then `index(action='refresh', force=True)`. | WHY: The answer states the write path refuses (not warns) when the process is stale and that the refusal ignores `force`, so a force flag cannot override it.

decisions.mark: states that the annotation RIDES ON EVERY QUERY REPLY rather than waiting to be asked for, and that it is empty on a current tool
decisions.detail: QUOTE: each query reply carries `staleness` only when there is something to report. ... A current index gets no notice at all. | WHY: The answer says the annotation is attached to every query reply and is absent when the index is current, which matches the item's substance. || QUOTE: each query reply carries `staleness` only when there is something to report. ... A current index gets no notice at all. | WHY: The answer says the staleness annotation is attached to every query reply automatically and is absent when the index is current.
